clips.text_zh: 睇到個post 真係喊出嚟。15年前擺1K入BTC 而家值9M USD，我擺入prop firm 就輸到仆街 🙏 又係學費啦 ok 不如直接all in BTC算。
clips.text_en_b1: If you invested $1,000 fifteen years ago today, here is what it would be worth now. Bitcoin would have grown to about $8,970,000. Nvidia would be worth roughly $735,000. Tesla would be around $231,000. Apple is only about $29,000. The S&P 500 gave you $8,400. And gold, the safe pick, is just $2,150. Bitcoin absolutely destroyed every other asset on the list.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread comparing 15-year returns on $1k across BTC, NVDA, TSLA, AAPL, S&P, gold

signal.rationale: Post implies BTC is the only trade that mattered; implicit long bias from the returns comparison

clips.text_en_b2: If you had invested a thousand dollars fifteen years ago, here is roughly what that position would be worth today. Bitcoin would have ballooned to around nine million dollars, whereas Nvidia would sit near seven hundred and thirty-five thousand. Tesla comes in at roughly two hundred and thirty-one thousand, while Apple only managed about twenty-nine thousand. The S&P 500 delivered roughly eight thousand four hundred, and gold, traditionally the safe bet, barely scraped two thousand one hundred and fifty.
clips.text_en_c1: The post itself was enough to bring a tear to one's eye. Had one allocated a mere thousand dollars to Bitcoin fifteen years ago, that position would now be worth roughly nine million, eclipsing every other asset under comparison. Nvidia would have appreciated to approximately 735,000 dollars, Tesla to around 231,000, while Apple languishes at a comparatively modest 29,000. The S&P 500, traditionally regarded as the benchmark of prudent investment, yielded a mere 8,400, and gold, the perennial safe haven, offers little more than 2,150. Bitcoin didn't merely outperform; it annihilated the field.
clips.text_en_c2: A retrospective on a fifteen-year horizon yields, as one viral post observes, results almost comical in their asymmetry. A modest thousand-dollar stake deployed in Bitcoin at inception would, by present reckoning, have appreciated to approximately 8.97 million dollars — a figure so vertiginous as to render its competitors not merely suboptimal but faintly absurd. Nvidia shares, the supposed darlings of the artificial intelligence boom, would have delivered a comparatively pedestrian 735,000. Tesla clocks in at roughly 231,000; Apple, that erstwhile paragon of compounding, a mere 29,000. The S&P 500, long vaunted as the prudent man's vehicle, would have produced a meagre 8,400. Gold — refuge of the timorous — sits at 2,150. One need hardly be a chartist to discern the verdict: Bitcoin, in absolute terms, demolished the field.

clips.text_zh: Cybercab 放落Robotaxi network 等佢自己跑，呢個真係passive income嘅終極形態。我而家survey 返工返到傻，車我自己都養唔起，買架Cybercab 幫我打工 ok 算啦lol 睇下啦先。
clips.text_en_b1: Someone on /biz/ is asking for a redpill on buying Tesla Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network as passive income. The idea is you buy the vehicle, register it on Tesla's robotaxi platform, and it earns money for you while you sleep.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread asking how to deploy Cybercabs on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income

signal.rationale: Robotaxi passive-income pitch is a long TSLA bull case tied to the Cybercab program

clips.text_en_b2: A poster on /biz/ is asking for a redpill on purchasing Tesla Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network as a source of passive income. The concept is straightforward: you buy the vehicle, register it through Tesla's robotaxi platform, and let it earn money for you while you sleep. Tesla has been promoting this vision aggressively as a way for ordinary people to generate automated income directly from their cars.
clips.text_en_c1: A poster on /biz/ is requesting a redpill on whether purchasing Tesla Cybercabs and deploying them across Tesla's Robotaxi network constitutes a viable passive-income strategy. The premise is straightforward enough: acquire the vehicle, register it on Tesla's autonomous platform, and let it generate revenue while its owner sleeps, thereby eliminating the labour component traditionally associated with asset utilisation. Tesla has been marketing precisely this vision, positioning individual car ownership as a conduit for automated, hands-off returns rather than a depreciating liability.
clips.text_en_c2: A /biz/ interlocutor has thrown the floor open for a thorough redpilling on Tesla's Cybercab and its putative role as a wholly passive income-generating asset, parked obediently on the Robotaxi network while its proprietor sleeps. The thesis is seductively simple: acquire the vehicle, register it on Tesla's proprietary platform, and let algorithmic dispatch and autonomous operation accrue revenue on one's behalf, unmediated by labour, untroubled by depreciation. Tesla, never shy of grandiloquent vision, has long marketed precisely this proposition as a democratised mechanism by which ordinary motorists might convert depreciating metal into appreciating cashflow. Whether such promises survive contact with regulatory reality, insurance actuarial tables, and the caprices of consumer demand remains, of course, a rather different question. For the moment, the idea persists as a tantalising secular fantasy.

The company also describes it as the most intelligent and aligned model they have ever shipped. This is being treated by the AI crowd as a major milestone moment.

signal.rationale: News observation on GPT-6 launch, no trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI has just launched GPT-6 Astra, its newest flagship model, and the company is officially declaring this the dawn of the AGI era. On benchmarks the model nearly saturates ARC AGI 3, while OpenAI also describes it as the most intelligent and aligned system they have ever shipped. The AI community is treating this release as a major milestone moment, although plenty of skeptics remain unconvinced.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship model, and the company is now openly declaring the advent of the AGI era. On benchmark evaluation, the system reportedly approaches saturation on ARC-AGI 3, a metric that has historically proven resistant to frontier models. OpenAI further characterises it as the most capable and aligned architecture it has ever shipped, a claim that the AI community has greeted as a watershed moment, though its broader implications remain subject to vigorous debate.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship architecture, and has done so with the rhetorical flourish customary at such junctures: the company now declares, with admirable confidence, that the long-anticipated era of artificial general intelligence has formally commenced. On standardised evaluations, the system reportedly approaches saturation on ARC-AGI 3, a benchmark previously regarded as a credible proxy for general reasoning. Internal characterisation further describes the model as the most intellectually capable and, crucially, the most thoroughly aligned system the laboratory has yet shipped — a phrase that, depending on one's priors, functions either as reassurance or as marketing boilerplate.

He says he saw large numbers of African and Indian arrivals at Helsinki airport, in Helsinki center, in Tampere, in Oulu, and even up in Rovaniemi near the Arctic Circle. He frames it as a tipping point for the country and asks what is going on in Finland.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread about immigration levels across Finnish cities from Helsinki to Rovaniemi
clips.text_en_b2: A /pol/ poster is venting about immigration in Finland following a recent trip. He claims he encountered large numbers of African and Indian arrivals not only at Helsinki airport and in Helsinki city centre, but also in Tampere, in Oulu, and even as far north as Rovaniemi near the Arctic Circle. He frames the situation as a tipping point for the country and openly wonders what on earth is happening to Finland.
clips.text_en_c1: A /pol/ contributor, recently returned from Finland, is voicing disquiet over what he describes as an accelerating demographic transformation. He reports encountering substantial numbers of African and Indian arrivals at Helsinki airport, throughout the city centre, in Tampere, in Oulu, and even as far north as Rovaniemi, situated within the Arctic Circle. For him, this concentration represents a tipping point whose long-term consequences Finland appears unwilling to confront, prompting the broader question of what trajectory European immigration policy is actually pursuing.
clips.text_en_c2: A /pol/ contributor, freshly returned from Nordic soil, has taken to the board to lament what he characterises as a demographic tipping point for Finland. His anecdotal inventory is, by his own admission, geographically exhaustive: substantial contingents of African and Indian arrivals at Helsinki-Vantaa, conspicuous presence in the capital's central districts, additional sightings in Tampere, Oulu, and — most damningly, given the implied affront to national mythology — in Rovaniemi itself, that Laplandish outpost proximate to the Arctic Circle. Whether such impressions constitute representative data or merely the selective collation of a predisposed traveller is a methodological question the poster declines to entertain. He poses instead a simpler, more rhetorical inquiry — what precisely is unfolding — leaving the broader European immigration question to ferment, as it has for some years now, unresolved.

clips.text_zh: 啲tech bro AI 訓練食晒server 資源，搞到個個又要返去買dedicated hardware lol。S15 我都冇時間睇，返完工返到屋企已經廢咗，睇replay就算 🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Anon is laughing at how AI techbros have taken over so much server capacity that companies now have to keep building dedicated consoles and PCs again. The old prediction was that everyone would just stream games through subscriptions, but now hardware is back in demand. He calls it jewbros vs techbros and finds the whole thing very ironic.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread mocking AI compute demand forcing a return to dedicated PC/console hardware
clips.text_en_b2: Anon is taking the piss out of how AI techbros have gobbled up so much server capacity that companies are now forced to keep building dedicated consoles and PCs again. The old prediction was that everyone would simply stream games through subscriptions, yet hardware demand has staged a remarkable comeback. He frames it as techbros versus the streaming crowd and finds the whole turnaround thoroughly ironic.
clips.text_en_c1: Anon finds considerable amusement in the fact that AI techbros have effectively commandeered so much server capacity that enterprises are once again compelled to invest in dedicated consoles and PCs. The prevailing wisdom had been that cloud-based game streaming would render local hardware obsolete, yet surging demand driven by artificial intelligence workloads has reversed that trajectory entirely. He frames the situation in distinctly irreverent terms, characterising it as jewbros versus techbros, and savours the irony that hardware has reclaimed its former primacy.
clips.text_en_c2: An anonymous /v/ contributor is finding, in the present AI infrastructure boom, a rather delicious irony. The same technical buccaneers who once prophesied a fully subscription-streamed gaming future — in which local hardware would become quaintly obsolete, rendered vestigial by the boundless generosity of cloud compute — have, in their insatiable consumption of server capacity for training workloads, inadvertently resurrected the very market they sought to bury. Console manufacturers and discrete GPU vendors, dismissed not long ago as dinosaurs shuffling towards extinction, now find themselves unexpectedly back in capital expenditure conversations. The pundit, unable to resist the symmetry, frames the episode as techbros versus jewbros in a tableau whose poetic justice he finds quietly irresistible. As for Season 15 itself, his exhaustion after the working day renders live engagement aspirational; replays, mercifully, remain.

He started skinnyfat at 140 pounds, bulked up to 200, and has since cut back down to where he is now. He acknowledges his frame runs small, so he piles on extra shoulder work to compensate. clips.text_en_c1: A fitness-oriented poster is soliciting feedback on his present physique, currently standing at 5'9 and 160 pounds after two years of consistent training. He began his journey in a skinnyfat condition at 140 pounds, executed a bulk that carried him to 200, and has since executed a measured cut to his current weight. Cognisant of his narrow frame, he deliberately prioritises shoulder development to create the illusion of broader proportions. Daily intake comprises 160 protein, 272 carbohydrates, and 57 fat, totalling 2,293 calories, supplemented by over ten thousand paces.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ regular is soliciting critique of his current conditioning, having supplied the customary biometric dossier in service of informed response. At five foot nine and a hundred and sixty pounds after two years of resistance training, he represents the familiar trajectory of the formerly skinny-fat trainee: an initial bulk from 140, an admittedly enthusiastic ascent to 200, and a subsequent, more measured cut to present weight. Cognisant that his skeletal frame offers modest leverage, he has accordingly devoted disproportionate volume to deltoid development, that eternal compensatory pursuit of the narrow-clavicled lifter. His nutritional regimen is, by macro-counting standards, exemplary: 160 grammes of protein, 272 of carbohydrates, and 57 of fat, totalling 2,293 kilocalories, supplemented by daily step counts comfortably exceeding ten thousand. The verdict, one suspects, will be patient iteration rather than dramatic overhaul.

clips.text_en_b1: A first-time Demon Slayer viewer is on season 2 and confused about why the anime gets so much hate online. He points out that almost every criticism people make about it applies equally to other beloved shows. His theory is that Demon Slayer only gets attacked because it is extremely popular and made billions of dollars worldwide. He is enjoying the show anyway.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread from a first-time Demon Slayer watcher defending it against generic hate

signal.rationale: Anime culture discussion, no trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: A first-time Demon Slayer viewer, currently working through season two, is genuinely puzzled by the wave of online hate the series attracts. He argues that almost every criticism levelled against it could just as easily be aimed at other beloved shows. His theory is that Demon Slayer only gets attacked because it became insanely popular and raked in billions worldwide. He is still enjoying the show regardless.
clips.text_en_c1: A first-time viewer of Demon Slayer, currently midway through its second season, is perplexed by the volume of online hostility directed at a property that has generated billions in revenue worldwide. He contends, with some justification, that the criticisms levelled against it are equally applicable to numerous other celebrated series that escape comparable scrutiny. His working hypothesis is that Demon Slayer attracts disproportionate ire precisely because of its commercial success rather than any inherent artistic deficiency, a phenomenon he finds both predictable and mildly absurd.
clips.text_en_c2: A first-time viewer, currently wading through the second season of Demon Slayer, has registered bewildered dissent at the volume and vigour of online disparagement directed at a property whose commercial returns exceed, by any reasonable metric, the aggregate takings of most rival franchises combined. His counter-argument is disarmingly straightforward: virtually every stylistic and narrative objection routinely marshalled against the series — its formulaic structure, its perceived absence of subtext, its hyper-kinetic aesthetic — could be levelled, with equal facility, at numerous critically cherished antecedents. His working hypothesis, therefore, is that the hostility is itself a function of scale, that ubiquity invites resentment, and that Demon Slayer's billions function as provocation rather than validation.
